Table 1 presents the pattern-level mean scores (n = 15 patterns) for the UEQ-derived scales and the autonomy-focused items. Scores are classified as negative (M ≤ -1), neutral (-1 < M < 1), or positive (M ≥ 1) on the rescaled -3 to +3 range.

The UEQ-derived scales showed predominantly neutral ratings: on the UEQ composite, 14 of 15 patterns fell in the neutral range and only Nagging (M = -1.06) was negative.

Excluding Attractiveness, the UEQ-derived scales flagged only 3 patterns as negative (Nagging, Trick Wording, and Forced Access on Dependability; Nagging also on Stimulation), in contrast to the more negative picture produced by autonomy-focused items.

Autonomy-focused items revealed more consistently negative perceptions. Pressure (pressuring/suggesting) emerged as the most negative dimension (M = -1.08, SD = 0.72), with 8 of 15 patterns rated as pressuring. Deception (deceptive/benevolent) showed similarly strong negative perceptions (M = -1.03, SD = 0.64), with 6 patterns perceived as deceptive. Attractiveness (annoying/enjoyable, unfriendly/friendly) showed comparable negative ratings (M = -0.95, SD = 0.81), with the same 6 patterns rated as both unattractive and deceptive. Participants did not rate all dark patterns uniformly negatively. Deception ratings ranged from -2.09 (False Hierarchy, strongly deceptive) to +0.07 (Pull To Refresh, neutral), and Attractiveness from -2.15 to +0.58. Linear mixed models with a random intercept for participant confirmed that ratings differed across the 15 patterns, for Deception (F (14, 454.3) = 7.27, p < .001; 530 evaluations with a valid rating from 122 participants) and for Attractiveness (F (14, 505.6) = 12.98, p < .001; 576 evaluations from 124 participants); Kruskal-Wallis tests ignoring the clustering agreed (H (14) = 79.65 and 124.50, both p < .001). Ratings therefore varied substantially across patterns rather than clustering at a single negative value.

Research Question 1: Deception and Attractiveness Correlation

Among the four autonomy-focused items (pressure, addiction, covertness, deception), deception showed the strongest co-occurrence with attractiveness. Figure 1 displays this relationship across all 15 dark patterns. Deception ratings co-occur with attractiveness ratings (r = 0.93, p < .001, 95% bootstrap CI [0.80, 0.98]): patterns perceived as more deceptive were consistently judged as less attractive (more annoying, more unfriendly). This finding was robust to non-parametric assessment (ρ = 0.84, p < .001). higher values mean less deception (-3 = deceptive, +3 = benevolent); the axis is thus inverted relative to the dimension's name so that both dimensions' negative poles align, and the plotted values are the untransformed pattern means reported in Table 1.

Shared variance was r² = 0.86.

Robustness Checks.

Given n = 15 patterns, we assessed outlier influence.

Cook's distance flagged only Social Pressure (D = 0.32) as marginally exceeding the 4/n threshold; leave-one-out analysis changed r by at most ±0.025 (range: r = 0.90 to r = 0.95). The correlation was not driven by any individual pattern.

Pattern-Specific Observations. Six patterns were rated as both unattractive (M ≤ -1) and deceptive (M ≤ -1). Ordered from strongest to weakest deception perception, they were: False Hierarchy (M Decep = -2.09, M Attr = -2.05), Toying with Emotion (-1.97, -2.15), Trick Wording (-1.76, -1.83), Nagging (-1.58, -1.85), Forced Access (-1.53, -1.57), and Expectation Result Mismatch (-1.28, -1.18). The three strongest deception perceptions all belonged to the Interface Interference category.

Pull To Refresh sat at the other end of the distribution: it was the only pattern whose deception (M = 0.07) and attractiveness (M = 0.58) means lay above the scale midpoint, although both values fall within the neutral range (nine patterns were neutral on deception and nine on attractiveness). This point sits on the same regression line as the other 14 patterns rather than contradicting it, reinforcing the r = 0.93 association.

Its addiction rating was separately negative (M = -1.00), indicating that participants identified its addictive mechanics even though they did not perceive the design intent as deceptive.

Specificity Analysis.

To examine whether this correlation was specific to deception or reflected general negativity, we computed pattern-level correlations Table 2 presents average within-category correlation coefficients for strategic categories containing multiple patterns. Two categories demonstrated substantial internal consistency: Interface Interference (r = 0.84) and Social Engineering (r = 0.68). These high correlations indicate that patterns sharing manipulation strategies were associated with similar user evaluations across dimensions. Interface Interference Consistency. The three Interface Interference patterns (False Hierarchy, Trick Wording, and Toying with Emotion) showed highly correlated evaluations (r = 0.84). Figure 2 illustrates this consistency: all three patterns were consistently rated as pressuring, deceptive, obstructive, annoying, and unfriendly.

Figure 3 shows the three Interface Interference mockups: False Hierarchy (button prominence), Trick Wording (misleading labels), and Toying with Emotion (guilt-inducing language). Despite these implementation differences, users perceived all three consistently across evaluation dimensions.

Social Engineering Consistency.

The six Social Engineering patterns (Gamification, Social Pressure, Social Connector, Content Customization, Endlessness, and Pull To Refresh) showed strong consistency (r = 0.68). These patterns leverage (a) False Hierarchy (b) Trick Wording (c) Toying with Emotion Figure 3 social proof, fear of missing out (FOMO), and engagement hooks to influence behavior.

Unlike Interface Interference's uniformly negative profile, Social Engineering patterns showed a mixed profile: ratings above the scale midpoint on Perspicuity and Efficiency (easy, clear, efficient) co-occurred with ratings below the midpoint on Pressure.

Obstruction Category. The Obstruction category showed no consistency (r = -0.11). These two patterns (Overcomplicated Process and Hindering Account Deletion) both obstruct user goals but through different mechanisms: Overcomplicated Process adds unnecessary steps and confusing language; Hindering Account Deletion imposes waiting periods and confirmation screens.

Sneaking Category.

The two Sneaking patterns showed moderate consistency (r = 0.46). Sneaking Bad Default and Expectation Result Mismatch both involve hiding information or presenting misleading expectations, but their profiles were less similar than those within Interface Interference or Social Engineering.

Exploratory: Which Items Isolate Which Categories

The four autonomy-focused items isolated different subsets of the 15 patterns.

Pressure was the broadest negative dimension (8 of 15 patterns rated as pressuring).

Deception was more selective and concentrated in Interface Interference. Addiction most cleanly isolated the Social Engineering patterns designed for prolonged engagement: Endlessness and Pull To Refresh were the only patterns rated addictive, with Gamification (M = -0.88) just inside the neutral range.

Discussion

User manipulation judgments appear closely tied to aesthetic response: the strong deception-attractiveness coupling (r = 0.93) extends moral-aesthetic links documented in psychological research to digital interfaces. Not every manipulation dimension behaves this way, and strategic categories cohere unevenly: Interface Interference and Social Engineering patterns are evaluated as coherent groups; Obstruction patterns are not, and Sneaking patterns only partly. At the pattern level, autonomy violations do not reduce to a single experiential quality.

Manipulation Perception and Aesthetic Judgment

The four autonomy-focused items do not behave as a single negativity scale.

Deception shows the strongest bivariate association with attractiveness (r = 0.93); pressure follows closely (r = 0.81, so the specificity claim is relative rather than categorical); covertness is moderate (r = 0.54); and addiction flips sign (r = -0.58), meaning patterns rated as more addictive are rated as more attractive. That sign reversal is the clearest evidence against an undifferentiated-negativity account: if participants were simply rejecting dark interfaces wholesale, no item would correlate the opposite way from the others. Instead, the specificity only becomes visible once the vocabulary is disaggregated. The pattern of correlations, rather than any single coefficient, is what indicates that the four items yield distinct pattern-level perceptual profiles (see Limitations for the participant-level caveat). This aligns with moral psychology research on intertwined aesthetic and moral judgments (Haidt, 2001), extending it to digital interfaces. Rather than judging deceptive interfaces solely as instrumentally problematic, users' aesthetic evaluations co-vary with their deception judgments, consistent with a more affective than deliberative process, akin to disgust responses to moral violations (Chapman & Anderson, 2013; Schnall et al., 2008). Processing-fluency accounts (Reber et al., 2004) offer a candidate mechanism: the perceptual and cognitive friction that typically accompanies manipulative interfaces may reduce fluency, and reduced fluency co-occurs with negative affect and aesthetic judgment.

Perceptual Coherence of Manipulation Strategies

User perception maps onto designer strategy unevenly. The high coherence of Interface Interference (r = 0.84) and Social Engineering (r = 0.68) shows that patterns in these categories received similar evaluation profiles even when surface implementations differ substantially (button styling vs. guilt language within Interface Interference; infinite scroll vs. gamification within Social Engineering). One possible interpretation is that users track shared underlying mechanisms (cognitive misdirection in the first case, social leverage in the second); the correlations themselves establish similarity of evaluations, not the mechanism behind it. The near-zero coefficient for Obstruction (r = -0.11; Sneaking was moderately coherent at r = 0.46) says something different: exit barriers and usability friction are grouped together by designer intent but were not evaluated alike; one interpretation is that they operate via psychologically distinct pathways. Category coherence is therefore a property of users' evaluations, not an automatic consequence of the designer's taxonomy.

Interface Interference as Cognitive Manipulation. The three Interface

Interference patterns (False Hierarchy, Trick Wording, Toying with Emotion) produced consistent evaluations despite substantial implementation differences (button prominence, misleading labels, guilt-inducing language). Ratings tracked together across these patterns and were uniformly negative across all evaluation dimensions (pressuring, deceptive, annoying, unfriendly), consistent with a shared strategic target: exploiting visual hierarchy and emotional framing to bias information processing.

Social Engineering's Mixed Profile.

Social Engineering cohered despite greater implementation diversity (Gamification, Social Pressure, Social Connector, Content Customization, Endlessness, Pull To Refresh), sharing reliance on social proof, FOMO, and engagement mechanics. Unlike Interface Interference, these patterns produced a mixed profile: positive ratings on traditional UX dimensions (easy, clear, efficient) co-occurred with negative autonomy ratings (pressuring, addictive). This duality may explain why such patterns persist: they deliver genuine usability benefits alongside mechanics users rate as addictive.

Obstruction's Failed Coherence. The near-zero within-category correlation for Obstruction (r = -0.11) is informative. Overcomplicated Process and Hindering Account Deletion both obstruct user goals but may involve different mechanisms: the former creates friction during ongoing use, while the latter imposes exit barriers salient only when users attempt to leave, a motivational state difficult to simulate from a static mockup. Obstruction, at least in our implementation, may group interfaces operating via distinct psychological mechanisms. The selective rather than uniform coherence across categories is difficult to attribute to a uniform response tendency alone, although our analyses do not formally rule out methodological explanations such as common-method variance or properties of the particular mockups chosen for each pattern.

Discriminating Judgment When Vocabulary is Provided

These findings complicate the assumption that users are "blind" to dark patterns (Sluijpers, 2022). When given evaluation vocabulary, participants' ratings differentiated manipulation-relevant dimensions, suggesting explicit vocabulary surfaces tacit evaluations. Articulated perception, however, need not translate into behavioral resistance.

The neutral Covertness ratings (M = 0.38; no pattern ≤ -1) argue against generalized negativity: users rated six patterns as deceptive and eight as pressuring yet judged none as covert. If participants had rejected dark interfaces wholesale, Covertness would have tracked Deception. Prior work documenting behavioral effects without corresponding UX deficits (Bongard-Blanchy et al., 2021) may reflect this measurement gap: standard frameworks emphasize dimensions on which Social Engineering patterns, for instance, averaged positive ratings (Perspicuity, Efficiency), while autonomy-focused items revealed what the standards obscured.

Practical Implications

For UX Evaluation. Traditional UX frameworks fail to surface manipulation dimensions that co-occur with aesthetic judgment. The UEQ composite flagged only 1 of 15 dark patterns as negative, yet users rated the same patterns as pressuring, deceptive, and unattractive when autonomy-focused vocabulary was available. We recommend augmenting standard evaluations with four autonomy items: perceived coercion (pressuring/suggesting), addictiveness (addictive/non-addictive, the item that most cleanly isolated Social Engineering patterns), covertness (covert/revealed), and deception (deceptive/benevolent).

For Regulation. The deception-attractiveness co-occurrence provides a user-perception signal for regulatory assessment: designs rated efficient yet unattractive may flag potential manipulation. Strategic coherence findings suggest a possible implication for scope: regulation could address coherent strategies (Interface Interference, Social Engineering) that users evaluate as unified approaches, rather than prohibiting individual patterns.

For Design Education.

Design education should explicitly connect aesthetics and ethics. Teaching designers that manipulation manifests as aesthetic unpleasantness may help internalize ethical considerations as intrinsic to aesthetic quality rather than external constraints.

Limitations

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, our study did not include non-manipulative control designs, so ratings cannot be anchored to a benign baseline.

Substantial variance across patterns mitigates this concern: deception ratings ranged from -2.09 (False Hierarchy) to +0.07 (Pull To Refresh), with significant differences across patterns in the mixed-model tests (p < .001). Pull To Refresh received the highest deception and attractiveness means (both within the neutral range), functioning as a de facto reference point, and the central correlation depends on relative ordering rather than absolute levels.

Second, we used mockups rather than functional prototypes. The neutral Covertness ratings and Obstruction's absent coherence likely reflect this: covert mechanics and exit-barrier manipulations require functional interaction to fully manifest.

Third, our sample skewed toward technically savvy users (87% self-reported technical savvy) residing predominantly in Austria (75%), with the survey administered in English and German. The tacit-awareness argument we develop here is one we would expect to be sensitive to design literacy and to the regulatory-discourse context our participants share (DSA, GDPR, ongoing dark pattern coverage), in which "manipulation" and "deception" are everyday descriptors. We can only speculate about how the deception-attractiveness coupling we observed would generalize to samples with less design literacy or different regulatory cultures; one possibility is that the coupling decomposes into an articulated and an affective component whose relative weights differ across populations, but we did not test for this. Cross-cultural accounts of felt manipulation (C. M. Gray et al., 2021) indicate that such perceptions can vary across cultural contexts, making replication across literacy strata and regulatory cultures a priority direction.

Fourth, we examined social media dark patterns specifically. Whether the deception-attractiveness association generalizes to other domains (e-commerce, health apps, financial services) remains an empirical question.

Fifth, our autonomy-focused items have not undergone formal psychometric validation. Our interpretive claims rest on pattern-level dissociation: across the 15 patterns the four items show different correlations with attractiveness (r = 0.93 for deception versus r = -0.58 for addiction), different distributions of negative ratings, and different alignment with strategic categories. We did not, however, establish participant-level discriminant validity, which would require larger per-pattern samples and confirmatory factor analyses; the constructs should therefore be read as pattern-level perceptual dimensions rather than as participant-level scales, and full scale validation is the primary direction we flag in Future Work. The development process drew on dark pattern literature and the approach of the Microsoft Desirability Toolkit (Benedek & Miner, 2002); practical utility was nonetheless evident: the autonomy items flagged 6 patterns as deceptive and 8 as pressuring, versus 1 flagged as negative by the UEQ composite.

Sixth, our correlational design cannot establish causality. Reverse causation (unattractive designs triggering suspicion) or a third unmeasured variable (e.g., general negativity toward the interface) could drive both aesthetic and deception judgments.

Experimental manipulations varying deception while controlling aesthetics would help distinguish these possibilities.

Future Work

Several directions follow. A first priority is formal scale development for the autonomy-focused items (confirmatory factor analysis, test-retest reliability).

Alternative antonyms should be compared psychometrically, for example deceptive/honest alongside deceptive/benevolent, and anti-addictive in place of non-addictive, testing whether explicitly positive poles allow the instrument to characterize "bright" as well as dark patterns. A full user-experienced ethics questionnaire, with subscales for pressure, covertness, and deception, would complement existing UX instruments.

Further directions include longitudinal research on whether aesthetic aversion diminishes as patterns become familiar; individual differences in the deception-unattractiveness association; and behavioral validation examining whether articulated perception predicts resistance to manipulation.

Pull To Refresh and the Normalization Hypothesis.

Pull To Refresh is an informative exception: the pattern rated least deceptive (M = 0.07) was also rated most attractive (M = 0.58), both within the neutral range, as the r = 0.93 correlation would predict, despite a negative addiction rating (M = -1.00). One possible explanation is a normalization hypothesis: patterns that become ubiquitous may cease to co-occur with deception-related aesthetic aversion even when addictive mechanics remain recognizable. Pull To Refresh is now standard across mobile interfaces; users may acknowledge its addictive quality while no longer perceiving the design intent as deceptive, possibly because the mechanism relies on motor habit rather than cognitive misdirection. If aesthetic-based manipulation signals diminish with exposure, proactive regulatory intervention may be necessary before novel patterns become entrenched.

Testing this hypothesis requires comparing familiar and novel implementations of the same mechanism.

Conclusion

The four autonomy-focused items we examined produced distinct pattern-level perceptual profiles rather than a single negativity scale. Deception ratings co-occurred strongly with negative aesthetic judgments (r = 0.93), while pressure, addictiveness, and covertness showed weaker or opposing associations. Several designer-intent groupings (Interface Interference, Social Engineering) map onto unified user experiences, and Pull To Refresh, a pattern rated addictive but least deceptive, is consistent with the possibility that familiarity erodes the aesthetic signal that ordinarily accompanies manipulation.

Standard UX instruments miss most of this. Autonomy-focused vocabulary makes it visible, without producing blanket negativity: participants discriminated between deception, pressure, addictiveness, and covertness. These results motivate the development and formal validation of ethics-focused UX measurement scales as a direction for future research on unethical design.
